title: Permit-as-Firmware Groundwater Pump Governor
one_liner: A smart pump controller that hard-enforces a farmer's groundwater allocation and lets an agent trade unused acre-feet with neighbors before the pump ever exceeds its limit.
customer: Irrigated growers (almonds, pistachios, alfalfa, wine grapes) in California's regulated groundwater basins, especially San Joaquin Valley subbasins with adopted allocations and overpumping penalties. Groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs) are the channel and co-payer.
problem: Allocations are enforced after the fact from meter reads. Kings County's agency, for example, set a $500-per-acre-foot charge for pumping above base allocation, with penalties slated after the 2026 water year. Probationary subbasins (Tule, Tulare Lake) add $300-per-well registration and a $20-per-acre-foot state fee. Farmers overshoot by accident, water trades run through brokers and phone calls, and GSAs cannot verify compliance without costly audits.
solution: A retrofit device on the well's starter or VFD, tied to a certified flow-meter reader, keeping a live allocation ledger. It soft-throttles as the budget nears zero, and can hard-stop with a paid override that 'borrows' at the penalty price. The grower's dashboard or agent can pre-bid to buy or sell units on a subbasin exchange. The GSA receives a read-only, tamper-evident compliance feed and can give fee discounts for participating wells.
why_now: Allocation-based enforcement begins in earnest with the 2027 water year, and the state has already put two San Joaquin Valley subbasins on probation. Water prices and fallowing pressure make trading valuable. Cellular and LoRa IoT and smart motor starters are now cheap.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per well install, $50-150 per month per well, a 1-2% fee on water trades, and GSA grants or fee credits that subsidise compliance metering.
non_obvious_insight: The law is already a constraint. The product turns a legal budget into a physical budget, like a hard credit limit on a card. Growers want the stop because it converts unpredictable $500-per-acre-foot penalties into a controllable budget, and GSAs want it because self-reporting becomes verified data. Sell it as insurance against fines, not as smart irrigation.
first_30_days: Pick one subbasin with adopted allocations and penalties. Recruit 3 pump-service companies as install partners, since they own the relationship with the well. Pilot free on 5 wells in exchange for testimonials and data. Ask the GSA general manager for a compliance-metering pilot grant.

title: A Price Index and Exchange for Agent Labor
one_liner: Publish the going rate and accuracy for standardized agent-delivered tasks (per 1,000 invoices, per verified ticket resolution), then let buyers run reverse auctions against it.
customer: CFOs, procurement and ops leaders at enterprises buying agent services, investors and analysts, and later the agent vendors that bid for work.
problem: Buyers have no reference price. Vendor pricing is opaque and shifting from seats to outcomes, quality varies widely, and Gartner says only about 130 of thousands of 'agentic' vendors are real. Unit token prices fell about 67% but bills rose, so nobody knows what a task should cost.
solution: Define standardized task classes with public test sets and acceptance criteria (invoice extraction and coding, tier-1 support resolution, KYC document review, meeting scheduling). Run blinded monthly bake-offs across vendors on hidden holdouts and publish a quality and cost-per-verified-outcome index. Sell buyer-side bake-offs on customers' own data. Later add an RFQ exchange with escrow released when acceptance tests pass.
why_now: Outcome pricing arrived in 2026, agent-washing is rampant, and benchmarks exist for models but not end-to-end vendors. Project Vend-style real-world evaluations show that outcomes need checklists and supervision to be trustworthy.
revenue_model: $20-$60k/year subscriptions for enterprises and investors, $15-$40k custom bake-offs, and a 3-5% exchange take rate later.
non_obvious_insight: Markets need a benchmark price before they need a marketplace, as freight and housing indices came first. Agent labor has large quality and price dispersion, and the party that publishes the reference sets the negotiation frame for the whole category.
first_30_days: Pick 2 task classes and assemble public plus holdout data. Run 6 vendors and publish the first index free with full methodology. Sell the first custom bake-off to a buyer and use it as a case study.

title: Regrade: Stamped Reclaimed Framing Lumber
angle: Pairing 2: Construction/housing shortage/trades labor/home services x Waste/recycling/circular economy/critical minerals/materials
one_liner: A mobile lumber re-grading and code-acceptance service that turns torn-out framing lumber from chip-pile waste into stamped, sellable studs and joists for ADUs, garages and additions.
customer: Deconstruction and demolition contractors and salvage yards (pay per board foot graded, or sell us stock). Small builders, ADU builders and remodelers buy packages.
problem: Framing costs are climbing (Austin framing up 25-50%, adding $2-5K per home, and builders estimate tariffs at about $10,900 per home). A 44-year median housing stock throws off tons of dimensional lumber, but yards cannot sell it for structural use because building officials want a grade stamp, so most of it is chipped for fuel or mulch at tens of dollars a ton.
solution: A truck-mounted setup with a certified grader, de-nailer and moisture scanner, working with an accredited grading agency or agency-approved third-party graders to re-grade and stamp. It also produces acceptance packets for local building departments. Sell 'ADU framing kits' and pre-nailed wall panels made from stamped reclaimed lumber at 20-35% below new.
why_now: Tariff-inflated lumber and a July 2026 ROAD to Housing Act that streamlines review for multifamily of 15 units or fewer and funds standard duplex/townhome plans should create a wave of small infill and ADU projects. Framing-crew scarcity also favors pre-made panels.
revenue_model: Grading fee per thousand board feet; margin on framing kits and panels; salvage purchases from deconstruction crews.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier to reuse is paper, not supply. Old true-dimension, slow-grown lumber often grades at or above new stock, and small builders' need for speed means the buyer will pay for panelization.
first_30_days: Confirm with an accredited grading agency and two local building departments what re-grade stamps and packets they accept. Hire a certified grader by the day. Contract 3 deconstruction crews for lumber. Sell one ADU frame or garage kit to prove code acceptance and margins.

title: Rainbows End Book Scanning With Chain of Custody
one_liner: Vernor Vinge's destructive mass digitization of a library, run as a service where the AI customer is owner of record and gets clean text plus a custody certificate, never resold scans.
customer: Specialist and mid-tier model builders (legal, medical, engineering and regional-language models) and enterprises training internal models. The buyer is the head of data or general counsel.
problem: After the Bartz v. Anthropic ruling (fair use for buying and scanning print books) and the $1.5 billion settlement over pirated copies, buy-and-scan is the defensible path. But it takes procurement across thousands of sellers, cutters, production scanners, QA and custody records. Only frontier labs have that muscle (the Project Panama disclosures in 2026 showed how large it was).
solution: Acquire books on the customer's behalf under a bill of sale so the customer is owner of record. Scan under work-for-hire, deliver OCR text and a chain-of-custody ledger (ISBN, invoice, copy serial number, cut and pulp certificate), and retain no digital copies. Focus on niches frontier labs skip: out-of-print trade and technical manuals, legal treatises, closing corporate and law-firm libraries, university deaccessions and regional-language books. A rare-edition triage rule sends scarce books to libraries or an archive instead of the cutter.
why_now: The Project Panama disclosures, the 2025 settlement and public backlash over 'book burning' have made provenance a line item for legal teams. Specialist labs want clean data but lack ops. Production scanners and hydraulic cutters are cheap and off the shelf.
revenue_model: Per-book fee (about $1.50-3), acquisition cost pass-through plus 10-20% procurement margin, typically $25-100k per project, plus a premium for custody-certificate audits.
non_obvious_insight: The Bartz reasoning covers a lab scanning books it owns for its own training, not reselling the scans. The whole business must therefore be structured as an agent working for the owner, not as a data vendor. The scarce input is not scanning but acquiring legally owned physical copies of niche material at scale, and the certificate is what counsel actually buys.
first_30_days: Spend about $25k on a hydraulic cutter and two production scanners. Buy about 10,000 books from library Friends sales and estate lots in one domain (for example legal treatises). Run a 5,000-book pilot for a legal-AI or medical-AI startup, using a custody-certificate template reviewed by copyright counsel.

title: Supervised-Hours Bench for Counselors and Social Workers
one_liner: A managed group-supervision network and hour-logging platform that lets clinics fund the thousands of post-degree supervised hours gating counseling, MFT and social-work licenses.
customer: Group therapy practices, community mental-health agencies and school districts hiring associate-level counselors and social workers; the associates themselves.
problem: Counseling, psychology and social work were excluded from the higher federal loan cap. Licensure typically requires 2-4k supervised hours after the degree, and associates often pay $50-150 an hour out of pocket for supervision that is scarce and tracked on paper. Clinics cannot hire associates faster than supervisors can be found.
solution: Certified supervisors, often semi-retired licensed clinicians, deliver state-compliant group supervision by video. The platform logs hours in board-ready format and enforces state ratios and rules. Clinics pay per associate per month to onboard associates who can bill insurance under supervision.
why_now: The July 2026 loan caps squeeze students in excluded fields and push them toward employer support. Behavioral-health demand is high, and telesupervision is widely permitted in many states after the pandemic.
revenue_model: $150-300 per associate per month from the clinic, supervision delivery margin, and hour-logging SaaS. Optional share of billed associate revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in the credential chain is not the degree but post-degree supervision, and the payer is the employer, not the student, because associates bill insurance and become revenue-positive once supervised.
first_30_days: Pick one large state that permits telesupervision. Recruit 5 licensed supervisors. Sign 3 group practices with about 10 associates in total. Run the hour logs in spreadsheets first and charge $200 per associate per month. Verify board rules before selling.

title: Own-Your-Office Buyer Groups for Practices
one_liner: Assemble dentists, clinics, law and accounting firms into buyer clubs that buy discounted vacant office buildings and split them into owner-occupied condos financed with SBA loans.
customer: Small professional practices renting 3,000-15,000 sf each (5-20 per building), plus special servicers and receivers who need a bulk exit for distressed office.
problem: National office vacancy is 17.8%, office CMBS delinquency 13.2%, $39B of office debt matures within 12 months and $289B by 2028 on about 14,000 properties. Sellers are forced, but institutional buyers price office as an income asset and few small buyers can act. Small practices keep paying roughly $33 asking rent with escalators and never see the building trade at a fraction of replacement cost.
solution: Pre-qualify 8-15 owner-users (financials and SBA 504/7(a) eligibility), find 40-150k sf Class B buildings from servicers at low per-sf bases, create a condo declaration and a single purchasing entity, close in bulk, then finance and deed units individually to practices (each occupying its own space). Keep the association-management and repositioning contract.
why_now: Servicers are actively seeking exits and most B/C buildings do not pencil for residential conversion, so owner-occupancy is the highest and best use. SBA programs finance owner-occupants at very high LTV, and high rates make a lease a large fixed cost relative to ownership.
revenue_model: 2-4% sponsor fee per unit sold, condo-ization margin or promote on unsold units, and recurring building/association management ($0.60-1.00 per sf per year) plus resale commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Investors value office on cash-flow multiples, while owner-users value it at the rent they would otherwise pay. At distressed bases the owner-user's willingness to pay can exceed the investor's bid, and no one is aggregating this fragmented demand against a forced-seller supply pool.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with cheap Class B office. Launch a landing page and outreach through dental, medical and CPA associations and SBA/CDC lenders. Collect 10 non-binding letters of intent from practices. Approach 2-3 servicer asset managers about bulk-sale listings. Charge a refundable $2,500 deposit for founding-member slots.

title: Verified-Offer Shield Against H-2A Recruitment Scams
angle: Pairing 2: Food & agriculture x Cybersecurity/deepfake fraud/identity verification/scams
one_liner: A WhatsApp-native registry where growers publish verifiable H-2A job offers and authorized recruiters, so workers can check any offer in seconds and growers get proof they never sanctioned a fee-charging middleman.
customer: Grower associations and large H-2A employers, plus farm labor contractors running H-2A programs, who pay per worker. Workers use it free.
problem: H-2A is scaling as the domestic workforce shrinks (over 300K visas in 2024; EPI expects growth toward 500K jobs after the Oct 2025 wage rule; the workforce reportedly fell by at least 155,000). Fake recruiters and impersonated grower pages sell nonexistent jobs or charge illegal fees. H-2A rules make employers contractually responsible for banning recruiter fees, so a scam in a grower's name is a compliance and reputation hit. Late or absent arrivals mean unharvested crops.
solution: Growers verify their business identity once, attach a DOL job-order number and issue a signed offer card with a QR and short code. Recruiters receive a 'licensed by grower' credential. A worker-side WhatsApp and SMS bot works in Spanish and through voice notes for Indigenous-language speakers (Mixtec, K'iche'). It replies 'verified', 'not found' or 'fee reported' and takes fee complaints. Growers get an audit trail of their recruiter chain and arrival tracking.
why_now: The immigration crackdown removed workers, and strawberry and almond growers reportedly lost up to 30% of crews in early 2026. The H-2A wage rule changed the incentives. AI makes fake job pages, voices and documents cheap. WhatsApp Business APIs are mature, and nobody in agriculture has a verification layer.
revenue_model: $15-40 per worker per season paid by the employer or association, a premium tier for recruiter-chain audit trails and DOL-ready records, and possible lender or insurer sponsorship.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the grower, not the victim. Growers carry the legal and commercial exposure to recruiter fraud and have the budget, while workers cannot pay. Verification for the poor is funded by the party with compliance liability.
first_30_days: Sign one grower association for a pilot with 3 member farms. Build the WhatsApp bot on the Meta Cloud API. Recruit 2-3 recruiter partners in Mexico and Guatemala. Collect 20 real scam examples through worker centers and legal-aid groups, and use them to demonstrate detection.

title: Human Reach Audits for Newsletter and Podcast Sponsors
one_liner: Bot- and agent-scrubbed reach certificates that let honest newsletters and podcasts charge sponsors for verified human eyeballs.
customer: Newsletter and podcast operators with $5k-200k/month in sponsorship revenue on the sell side, and B2B sponsors, creator agencies and marketplaces on the buy side.
problem: Cloudflare's CEO says bots are about 20% of traffic and will exceed human traffic by 2027, with agents hitting about 1,000x more sites than a human. Opens, clicks and downloads increasingly come from scanners and AI assistants, not people. B2B sponsors buying through marketplaces such as Passionfroot and Agentio will see CPA misses and disputes, and start discounting all creators. Honest operators are hurt most.
solution: Connect to the newsletter platform and podcast host logs (Beehiiv, Ghost, Mailchimp, Libsyn, Buzzsprout). Classify every open, click and download as human, scanner or agent using timing, IP ranges, user-agent patterns and hidden honeypot links. Issue a 'Verified Human Reach' certificate with methodology and monitor it monthly, plus a sponsor-facing verify link. Later, offer pricing per verified-human click.
why_now: The bot-share trend is now being stated by infrastructure CEOs, B2B creator marketplaces are scaling (Passionfroot $15M, Agentio $40M), and reader-side detection has entered the mainstream through Substack's Pangram scan. Sponsors are getting more skeptical this budget cycle.
revenue_model: $199-499 per audit, $99/month monitoring, marketplace API fees per certificate, and a performance fee on verified-human click pricing.
non_obvious_insight: The authenticity gap that moves money is not in the content but in the audience. Sponsors buy human attention, and a certificate lets honest creators earn a premium rather than being averaged down.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 sponsor-funded newsletters via Beehiiv and Substack communities and offer a free 'what percent of your clicks are bots' scan in exchange for publishing an anonymized benchmark. Sell certificates before their next media-kit refresh, and pitch two B2B marketplaces or agencies.

title: Medicare-First Longevity Kit for Independent Practices
one_liner: Longevity medicine built on what Medicare already pays for, sold as a workflow kit to independent primary-care practices.
customer: Independent primary-care and DPC-adjacent practices (2-15 clinicians) with 500-2,000 Medicare patients each.
problem: The longevity boom (Function $2.5B, Neko ~$7B, Superpower up to $349/yr) targets cash-paying under-55s, while the highest-risk group, seniors, has a covered prevention stack that is badly under-used. Well under half of beneficiaries take the Annual Wellness Visit, and independents lack the workflow to turn covered services into a healthspan program.
solution: A configurable 'healthspan AWV' template with functional tests (chair-stand, grip, gait speed), cognitive and falls screens, covered lipid, diabetes and bone screening, and vaccine gap-closing. A monthly care-management billing layer (APCM codes introduced in 2025). Compliant ABN-based cash upsells for ApoB or Lp(a). Practices get scripts, patient handouts and a collections dashboard.
why_now: APCM monthly primary-care codes are new (2025). The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge began Jul 1, 2026, pulling seniors into metabolic care. Cash longevity prices keep rising, which cedes the 65+ segment. About 82% of doctors are employed, so the remaining independents are underserved by digital vendors.
revenue_model: $600-1,200/month SaaS per practice plus 15-20% of incremental collected revenue (est. $30-80k per clinician per year of newly captured billing).
non_obvious_insight: 'Longevity' for the 65+ is mostly a billing-and-workflow problem on already-covered benefits. Founders build for cash because that is where the venture buzz is, and they overlook the biggest and sickest demographic, whose payer is already at the table.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 independent practices via state IPAs and DPC-Medicare communities. Offer a free 30-day audit of their AWV and care-management capture, pulled from claims, showing dollars left on the table. Convert to a $499/month pilot with a success fee.

title: Gauntlet Rehearsal Range for Drone Startups
one_liner: A private test range that reproduces the Drone Dominance Gauntlet scoring so new entrants can rehearse, fail cheaply and qualify before the real event.
customer: Drone makers preparing for Gauntlet 2.5, 3 and 4, from Series A startups to hardware teams entering defense for the first time.
problem: In Gauntlet 1 only 24% of drones reached 10 km, and even in Gauntlet 2 only 11 platforms hit 15 km. Each event has a limited slot count, roughly 6 months apart. New entrants burn scarce runs discovering avoidable failures, and few have range access or scoring instrumentation.
solution: Lease land and airspace near a Front Range site and instrument it to the published Gauntlet metrics (range, sortie count, jamming, payload, ease of operation). Sell run-blocks with independent data logs, a failure-mode report and a readiness score.
why_now: About 60,000 drones will be ordered from winners, and the 200,000-unit target by 2027 pulls in dozens of new entrants. The Gauntlet cadence is public, and a wave of Gauntlet 2.5 bomber-drone entrants is forming now.
revenue_model: $8-25K per run-block, $60-120K seasonal packages, and a sponsor arrangement with primes or investors who want pre-screened suppliers.
non_obvious_insight: When a market runs on tournaments, the money goes to the rehearsal facility that every contestant needs. This is the pick-and-shovel of a public competition schedule.
first_30_days: Publish the Gauntlet 2 metrics as a public scorecard and lease a private test site with a landowner. Buy a few reference drones and a logging stack. Sell 3 startups a pre-Gauntlet 2.5 block.

title: Spindle-Hour Options: Reserve Capacity, Skip Inventory
one_liner: Standardized capacity-reservation contracts that let OEMs hedge supply risk by paying a small premium for guaranteed machining hours.
customer: Procurement leads at $50M-$1B OEMs (industrial equipment, medical devices, defense subcontractors) and 10-100 person job shops with idle spindles.
problem: 57% of negative ISM comments cite price volatility, and one respondent called lead times worse than the pandemic era. Machine-shop owners report buying a full year of inventory to lock in prices. That ties up cash and risks obsolescence. Marketplaces sell only spot capacity, and shops cannot get predictable base load.
solution: A standard reservation contract by machine class (3-axis, 5-axis, Swiss, wire EDM, weld cell). The buyer pays a reservation fee for N hours a month over 6-12 months at a strike rate, with materials indexed to published metals prices. The buyer exercises by releasing drawings within 10 days. The platform vets shops, holds deposits in escrow, and resells unexercised hours to spot buyers.
why_now: Metals repricing under Section 232, Hormuz freight shocks, machinery hiring picking up, and auto-supplier capacity going idle. Buyers can no longer count on spot capacity appearing.
revenue_model: 6-10% of reservation fees plus 2-3% of exercised work. Later, underwrite a portfolio of options for the spread.
non_obvious_insight: A job shop's most valuable asset is certainty of base load, and it will discount 10-20% for take-or-pay. Buyers fear not getting parts more than they fear price. An option on capacity is a cheaper hedge than a year of inventory, and the deposit doubles as working capital for the shop.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 shops with one machine class in one region (for example Northeast Ohio). Draft a two-page contract with a manufacturing lawyer. Pitch 15 buyers who are already stockpiling inventory. Aim for $50k in reservations by day 60. Run it as a brokerage first.

title: Loss-Curve Intelligence for Autonomous Trucking Insurance
one_liner: A benchmark and risk-scoring workbench that helps insurers, brokers and carriers price driverless-truck coverage using evidence instead of 'unknown'.
customer: Specialty insurers and reinsurers, MGAs, brokers, and large trucking carriers. AV operators such as Aurora, Kodiak, Bot Auto and Gatik also buy, to lower their premiums.
problem: Insurers price AV trucks 'slightly above' human drivers purely because of the unknown, with premiums expected to fall 15-25% a year. Werner's CIO says 'we have a gap' on pricing. Nobody has normalized exposure data by operating domain.
solution: Ingest public crash reports (NHTSA Standing General Order and state reports), published safety cases and operator-contributed telemetry. Build frequency and severity priors by operating design domain (lane type, speed, weather, time of day) and deliver a quarterly benchmark plus a route and lane risk-scoring API. Later, underwrite as an MGA.
why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and 500k+ driverless miles, the first real exposure data, and targets 30,000 trucks by 2030. Insurers must reprice yearly and need evidence to justify each step down.
revenue_model: $75-250k a year in subscriptions from insurers and reinsurers, per-policy data fees, and MGA commission (10-15% of premium) once loss data supports it.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not too few miles but the lack of a standard exposure unit. Whoever defines miles by operating domain as the accepted denominator becomes the FICO of autonomy, and operators will share data because it lowers their premiums.
first_30_days: Build an ODD-normalized frequency table from public NHTSA data. Interview 15 trucking and AV underwriters, send a free 'AV vs human benchmark' brief to 3 brokers, and close one $30k paid pilot with an MGA.

title: Clickwrap Gatekeeper: Agents Buy Contract Counsel
one_liner: An API agents call before clicking 'I agree'. It returns clause-level risk against the principal's delegated-authority policy, plus a signed archive of exactly what was accepted.
customer: Wallet-holding consumer and enterprise agents, and the platforms that run them, paying $0.02-$0.50 per document evaluation plus an evidence-archive fee per acceptance. Agent-wallet and browser-agent vendors are the natural embedders.
problem: Agents will accept tens of thousands of ToS, DPAs, auto-renewals, arbitration waivers and data-resale clauses for people and companies. Courts increasingly treat automated assent as binding, so the open legal question is the scope of the agent's authority. Agents can read a contract, but none has a legal-grade policy engine or a defensible evidence trail. Amazon's fight with Perplexity over agent access is one visible example of that unsettled authority.
solution: check(url_or_text, policy) diffs the document, hash-cached and versioned, against the principal's policy: max liability, no auto-renew beyond 30 days, no mandatory arbitration, no resale of personal data. It returns ALLOW, ESCALATE or REFUSE with cited clauses. On ALLOW it snapshots the page (hash, timestamp, screenshot) into a tamper-evident log so the principal can later prove what was accepted. A diff feed alerts the principal when terms change on services already accepted. It is positioned as a policy engine, not legal advice, with law-firm-authored policy packs.
why_now: Agent authority is the live legal question of 2026, with law-firm memos on 'authority to bind' and litigation over agent access. Payment protocols such as AP2 mandates and ACP mean agents now click through payment terms without a human present. Browser agents are in production use.
revenue_model: Metered evaluation (first-seen documents priced high, cache hits nearly free), an evidence-archive fee per accepted contract, enterprise policy packs, and a marketplace for lawyer-written policy templates with a revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of legal risk in the agent economy is not the model's hallucination but the tiny irrevocable assent. Because most ToS are near-identical templates, one shared cache amortizes legal analysis across millions of agents, which no single company can do for itself. Lawyers become policy authors rather than reviewers, and gross margin exceeds 90% once the cache is warm.
first_30_days: Crawl and index ToS, privacy and DPA pages for the top 5,000 SaaS and e-commerce sites and cluster them into templates. Publish a free MCP server with 1,000 free checks. Recruit 3 advisory lawyers to seed policy templates. Pitch agent-wallet startups and browser-agent vendors to embed it as a pre-payment check, and start charging in month 2.

title: Tele-Operated Night Aides for Small Care Homes
angle: Pairing 1: Aging/silver economy x Logistics & physical automation
one_liner: Metered remote-aide hours operating an off-the-shelf mobile manipulator robot in 6-16 bed residential care homes, so labor crosses borders when workers cannot.
customer: Owners of small residential care homes and assisted living homes (adult family homes, RCFEs) that run one awake overnight staffer, paying about $2,500-4,000 a month per home.
problem: Staffing is collapsing, with a 75-country visa pause, Haitian TPS loss and Wisconsin homes closing wings. One Wisconsin operator spent $100k+ on housing for overseas workers and then lost visa access. Small homes cannot buy robots or hire tech staff, and much aide time is walking, fetching and watching.
solution: Lease a wheeled mobile-manipulator (for example a Hello Robot Stretch-class unit) and pair it with remote aides, offshore or US-based. The remote aide handles night rounds, door and light tasks, supply fetching and two-way calming talk with dementia residents. The aide escalates to the on-site caregiver through a shared protocol. Do not touch medication or personal care.
why_now: Teleoperated home robots (1X NEO, Waymo-style remote centers) proved the model in 2025-26. Workers can no longer be moved, but work can. Occupancy is at a 19-year high with no new supply before 2030.
revenue_model: Monthly subscription per home covering robot lease plus a pool of remote hours. Overage billed per hour. Target unit margin of about 40% after remote-labor cost.
non_obvious_insight: Staffing rules count bodies on site, but most overnight risk is watching and fetching, which a remote human plus a modest robot can cover. The visa crackdown turns labor arbitrage into a physical-presence product.
first_30_days: Sign three care homes in one state that allow tech-augmented overnight staffing. Buy one robot and hire two remote aides. Run supervised night shifts and log fall and wandering response times as proof for the next 20 sales.

title: Pre-Engineered Single-Stair Plan Sets
one_liner: License stamped, fire-marshal-ready plan sets for 4-6 story single-stair buildings so small developers can use the new law without a $250K custom design.
customer: Small infill developers, church and nonprofit landowners and small architecture firms in single-stair states, plus modular fabricators.
problem: Seven states reformed single-stair rules in 2025 and Michigan followed in July 2026, promising about 10% cost savings, but architects and fire officials lack templates. Custom design is slow, local amendments add friction, and construction inputs are up 8.9% while multifamily starts fall.
solution: Engineered plan sets (4/5/6-story, 16-40 units, light-frame and mass-timber variants) with structure and MEP, a fire-safety compensation package, code narrative and a pre-meeting deck for local fire marshals. A network of local architects of record adapts them per site, and a per-state cost estimate is included.
why_now: New laws are taking effect (Michigan July 2026) and California AB 2074 awaits signature, while rising costs make small builders desperate for certainty.
revenue_model: $25-45K per plan license, $10-20K adaptation fee, referral fees from lenders and contractors, and a subscription for code updates.
non_obvious_insight: Legalization does not build housing; templates and fire-marshal comfort do. The first stamped precedent in each state becomes the local pattern, and plan sets have near-zero marginal cost.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed architect who has single-stair experience. Draft one 4-story 16-unit set for Michigan. Presell three licenses to small developers at a $15K founder price and schedule a meeting with one fire marshal.

title: Buy the Orphaned License of Dead Models
one_liner: Acquire or secure exclusive commercial-licensing rights to hugely downloaded open models and tools whose company died, then sell clean, warranted commercial licenses plus a public orphan-license registry.
customer: Startups and mid-size companies shipping voice features (dubbing, audiobooks, IVR, game NPC voices, accessibility) on top of XTTS-class models, and the procurement or legal teams of their enterprise buyers who now ask for model-license provenance.
problem: Coqui XTTS-v2 is still pulled about 6.75M times a month under a non-commercial license (CPML), but Coqui shut down in Dec 2023. Commercial licensing was 'available upon inquiry' from a company that no longer exists, so builders either violate the license, ship legal risk to customers, or rip out the best multilingual voice-cloning model. GitHub threads asking about commercial use or the license after shutdown were closed 'wontfix'.
solution: Phase 1: trace the rights chain (Coqui Inc., founders, assignees, any bankruptcy or dissolution filings) and option an exclusive commercial-licensing agency deal or outright IP purchase, which should be cheap because the seller is a dead startup. Phase 2: sell per-product annual commercial licenses ($2k-$25k) with a written rights-chain warranty and an audit letter that customers can hand to enterprise procurement. Phase 3: publish an Orphan Model Registry (model, steward status, license, who can grant commercial rights) as a free lead-gen asset and a paid API for AI-governance tools. Fallback if the rights-holder refuses: sell a fixed-price license-risk audit and a swap-to-permissive-model migration (Apache/MIT TTS) with regression tests.
why_now: Enterprise AI-governance questionnaires in 2026 ask for model and data provenance. The $1.5B Anthropic authors settlement (2025) and the Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (HN front page 2026-09-27, 626 points) made license hygiene a board-level topic. Open voice tools are exploding: VoiceStudio hit 43.9k stars, +27k in one month, and its README warns each bundled model has its own license to review before commercial use.
revenue_model: Annual per-product licenses ($2k-$25k), enterprise-wide licenses, audit and migration fees ($3k-$8k fixed price), registry API subscription ($200-$1k a month).
non_obvious_insight: Demand is already proven and supply is literally zero: nobody can sell a commercial license because the seller is dead, so dead-startup IP is the scarcest cheap asset in open AI. Evidence: XTTS-v2 shows 6,752,613 downloads last month under CPML (https://huggingface.co/coqui/XTTS-v2). Coqui repo issues on commercial use, license after shutdown and 'Move to MIT' are closed wontfix (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues?q=commercial+license+is%3Aissue). Issue #4022, opened nearly a year after shutdown, says the community is confused about 'commercial use and fine-tuning' (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues/4022). HN, Nov 2023: XTTS stays non-commercial with commercial licensing 'upon inquiry'. VoiceStudio's AGPL repo warns model licenses vary (https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio).
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pull Delaware and other corporate records for Coqui Inc., message the founders and former staff, and draft a one-page option agreement (small cash plus revenue share). Days 1-10: build the registry from 50 popular non-commercial or orphaned models on Hugging Face. Days 10-30: email companies that opened XTTS licensing issues and companies whose products visibly use XTTS (from public GitHub dependency graphs) with a $3k risk audit, and aim for 3-5 paid audits. If the rights option lands, convert those audits into licenses.

title: Church-Basement Microschools for Retired Teachers
one_liner: A turnkey venue, insurance, fire-code and ESA-billing kit that lets a retired teacher open an 8-15 student paid school in a congregation's empty weekday classrooms.
customer: Retired or soon-to-retire teachers aged 55-70 pay a monthly fee and a share of tuition. Congregations are the landlords. Parents are the end payers, through education savings account (ESA) funds.
problem: Microschool builders assume curriculum and tech are the hard part. What actually kills these schools is the certificate of occupancy and zoning, the fire marshal, liability insurance, ESA vendor approval and reimbursement paperwork, and bookkeeping. Retired teachers have the credibility and skills but no business experience. Meanwhile congregations hold Sunday-school classrooms that sit empty Monday to Friday and need rent.
solution: A state-by-state permit packet (occupancy class, what the inspector will actually ask for). A pre-negotiated group liability policy for microschools. A standard five-day lease with congregations covering rent, cleaning, security and safeguarding. Onboarding for ESA and voucher programs (including any accreditation or approved-provider requirements) plus back-office billing and attendance. A menu of curricula so the teacher chooses. A shared bench of substitute retired teachers for sick days.
why_now: Texas launched its Education Freedom Accounts in fall 2026 with $1 billion, about $10,474 per student in 2026-27 (a 12-student school is roughly $125k in revenue), and about 600 private schools and pre-K providers applied in the first 10 days. Universal or near-universal ESAs are live in a growing list of states, and a federal scholarship tax credit begins in 2027. About 1.5 million students are already in microschools, and teacher retirements are climbing.
revenue_model: $199-$399/month platform fee per school, about 4% of tuition processed, insurance commissions, and a 5% lease-admin fee from congregations.
non_obvious_insight: Pension re-employment caps generally bite when you return to a covered public district. Working for yourself in a private school usually does not touch your annuity (verify by state), and past full retirement age the Social Security earnings test no longer applies. So a retired teacher can keep her pension and collect full tuition. Parents' top trust signal is 'Mrs. Alvarez taught 31 years at Lincoln Elementary.' A church building that is already zoned, already inspected for children, and rents for $800-$1,500 a month is the cost moat. Curriculum is commodity. Occupancy and insurance are the moat.
first_30_days: In Texas or Arizona or Florida, recruit a cohort of 10 retired teachers through retired-educator associations and Facebook groups. Line up 5 congregations with weekday space. Build the permit checklist for one city, get one group insurance quote, and sign 3 pilot schools at $299/month. Target the January 2027 semester and the early-2027 ESA application cycle for 2027-28, since fall 2026 enrollment has already closed.

title: Pay the Grandmother: Relative-Care Subsidy Enrollment
one_liner: A multilingual concierge plus verified-attendance software that turns unpaid grandparents and relatives into subsidy-paid, health-and-safety-cleared caregivers, billed per enrollment to states and referral agencies.
customer: State child-care subsidy (CCDF) lead agencies, county subsidy offices and child care resource and referral (CCR&R) agencies. Secondary: workforce boards and Head Start grantees.
problem: Deserts are measured in licensed slots (3+ kids per slot), but most parents actually cobble together relative care that the maps never count. Many states can already pay license-exempt relatives through subsidy. Families don't enroll because of fingerprinting, training, provider agreements and slow payment. States are also wary of fraud (federal subsidy-fraud scrutiny in winter 2025-26, from memory, not verified). So the 'supply' looks empty while grandmothers work for free.
solution: A guided onboarding flow in the caregiver's language covers document collection, fingerprint appointment booking, CPR and safe-sleep micro-training, and e-signed provider agreements. Attendance is logged by phone tap-in with geo-stamp and parent co-sign, which gives the state verified attendance. Payment goes out by direct deposit or prepaid card within days. A state dashboard shows 'real supply unlocked' by county.
why_now: Childcare costs hit about $13,128 a year (up 29% since 2020) while licensed supply barely grows (centers +1.5%, homes +4.3% in 2024). The 2024 federal CCDF rule (7% copay cap, enrollment-based prospective payment) is being implemented by states in 2025-26 (from memory). Universal-care promises (NYC per the brief) create demand for supply that needs no buildings. Fraud scrutiny makes verified attendance a selling point, not a cost.
revenue_model: Per completed enrollment fee ($150-400) plus a per-active-caregiver monthly fee ($3-8), paid by the agency under a pilot contract. Pilots run $30-60k per CCR&R or county.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in childcare deserts is not buildings or workers. It is unpaid supply that already exists, blocked by paperwork and by states' fear of fraud. The winner sells verified attendance as much as enrollment.
first_30_days: Pick two states with permissive relative-care rules. Map every enrollment step and drop-off point. Offer one CCR&R a free 25-family concierge pilot run over WhatsApp and phone, with Twilio and a no-code form behind it. Recruit through Spanish-, Somali- and Hmong-speaking community groups. Get a letter of intent from one county for a paid per-enrollment fee.

title: Disposable Ocean Drifters Reporting Through Orbit
one_liner: $10-30 drifting sensors dropped from passing ships that report through Bluetooth-to-satellite links, building a dense ocean nowcast.
customer: Weather-routing companies, offshore wind and energy operators, hurricane-season shipping and fishing fleets, insurers and coast guards.
problem: Ocean observation is sparse and expensive, because standard buoys cost thousands of dollars each, and some public observing networks have reportedly lost capacity. Routing and offshore-operations customers pay for better current, wave and sea-surface data.
solution: A disposable floating sensor (GPS, temperature, basic wave motion) that uses a standard Bluetooth chip and a Bluetooth-to-satellite network for uplink. Recruit ships of opportunity (research vessels, yacht races, cargo lines) to deploy hundreds. Sell a nowcast layer and event-specific coverage such as hurricane drifts.
why_now: Hubble Network (6 satellites, $200M Series C) shows ordinary Bluetooth chips can reach orbit, and its next generation improves link margins. Sensors and uplink are now cheap enough for disposable use.
revenue_model: Data subscriptions $20-100k per year per routing or offshore customer. Event campaigns of $50-200k. Sensor kits sold at cost to research and racing fleets.
non_obvious_insight: Cheap satellite uplink flips ocean sensing from a few expensive fixed buoys to millions of throwaway ones, and ships already crossing the ocean provide free deployment.
first_30_days: Build 50 prototype drifters and test the link at sea on a partner yacht or research cruise. Sign two weather-routing or offshore wind customers for paid pilots before the next hurricane season.

title: Elder-Intelligible Voice for Healthcare AI Calls
one_liner: An audio layer that reshapes AI-agent voices so listeners 75+ with age-related hearing loss actually understand phone calls, sold per minute to healthcare voice-agent companies.
customer: Healthcare voice-AI vendors, pharmacies, payers and IVR providers whose outbound calls mostly reach people over 70.
problem: Voice agents are being deployed to call seniors about refills, discharge follow-ups and plan outreach. TTS is tuned for young ears, and phone audio cuts off above roughly 3.4 kHz, which is exactly where age-related hearing loss erases consonants (s, f, th, sh). Seniors mishear dates and doses, get frustrated and hang up. The vendor logs it as 'low engagement' and blames the patient.
solution: A drop-in post-processor between the TTS engine and the telephony stream: clear-speech prosody (slower on key phrases, pauses, sharper consonant timing), spectral reshaping tuned to typical presbycusis profiles, and optional per-caller calibration ('say the number you hear'). Add built-in comprehension checks like read-back of the dose. Prove it with a benchmark from a paid panel of 100 older listeners that shows word-recognition gains, then ship it as an API billed per audio minute.
why_now: Healthcare voice agents scaled fast in 2025-26 and their audience is old. Research already shows a clear-speech intelligibility benefit for synthetic voices. Low-latency neural audio processing is now cheap, and no one yet owns the psychoacoustics layer that sits under all those voices.
revenue_model: $0.01-0.03 per audio minute as an add-on, with enterprise minimums of $2-5k/month. Paid listening-panel certification packages (~$15k) that customers can cite in compliance and sales.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats 'voice for older adults' as a warmth and tone problem. It is a psychoacoustics plus telephony-bandwidth problem, and the fix is measurable in word-recognition scores, which makes it sellable. Older listeners can't tell they are the problem, so they just stop answering.
first_30_days: Recruit 30-40 adults 75+ from senior centers, paying $25 for a 40-minute listening test. Build a prototype on open-source TTS plus clear-speech DSP. Publish the intelligibility gain as a 2-page brief. Pitch 15 healthcare voice-agent startups with a free A/B test on 500 calls and aim to sign 2 paid pilots.
